analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Jones Act requirement that ships moving goods between U.S. ports be American-built and crewed.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2020 with no cosponsors and died in committee without a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Jones Act requires any vessel carrying cargo or passengers between U.S. ports — including to and from Puerto Rico — to be built in the United States, mostly U.S.-owned, and largely crewed by Americans. This bill would repeal those rules, letting foreign-built and foreign-crewed ships carry goods on domestic routes. Supporters say that would cut shipping costs, especially for Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska; opponents say it would cost U.S. shipyard and merchant marine jobs and weaken the nation's fleet.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska, and other non-contiguous areas pay higher shipping rates under the Jones Act because a limited fleet of U.S.-built ships is more expensive to build and operate; repeal would allow cheaper foreign-flag competition on those routes. Retailers, farmers, energy shippers, and households that bear freight costs would see prices ease where shipping is a big share of cost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shippers and consumers in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the coastwise laws known as the Jones Act, which require vessels carrying merchandise or passengers between U.S. ports, including to and from Puerto Rico, to be built in the United States, at least 75% U.S.-citizen owned, and mostly U.S.-citizen crewed.

Removing those requirements would allow foreign-built and foreign-crewed vessels onto domestic shipping routes, where their lower construction and operating costs would put downward pressure on freight rates that are currently set in a market closed to foreign competition.
Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska depend on ocean shipping for nearly all goods, so they bear the steepest Jones Act cost premium and would see the largest savings.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. shipyards, which sell most of their large commercial vessels into a protected domestic market, would lose their guaranteed customer base. American merchant mariners and the unions representing them would face competition from lower-wage foreign crews, and U.S.-flag operators would lose the reserved cargo. Supporters of the Jones Act also argue the country would lose trained crews and ships available for military sealift in a crisis.
analysis.who_pays_short: U.S. shipyards, merchant mariners, maritime unions

drawbacks.text: Repeal would expose U.S. merchant mariners and shipyard workers to direct wage and job competition from foreign-flag operators that can crew and build ships far more cheaply, eliminating a set of protected American jobs rather than just a price markup.

The Jones Act fleet and its crews are the basis for U.S. commercial sealift capability that the military draws on in wartime; full repeal with no transition or replacement would reduce that capacity, a cost the bill text does not address.
The bill is an outright repeal with no phase-in or compensation for affected workers and shipyards, so the adjustment burden would fall entirely and immediately on the industry it displaces.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Repeal would deliver real, broad savings to consumers and shippers, concentrated in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska, but the cost is not trivial: protected shipyard and mariner jobs would go, and the bill offers no transition or plan to preserve the sealift capacity the military relies on. A narrower bill — easing the build requirement while keeping U.S. crews, or compensating the affected workforce — would have balanced the ledger better; this one simply eliminates the protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then a subcommittee, sat there for the final two weeks of the Congress, and expired when the session ended with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Justin Amash introduced the Jones Act Repeal Act on December 17, 2020, the final month of the 116th Congress.
It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and, the next day, to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and no further action was taken.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S. shipbuilding industry, U.S.-flag shipping operators, and maritime labor unions came out ahead: the Jones Act's protected domestic cargo market remains fully in place, and consumers in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska continue paying the resulting freight premium.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: U.S. shipyards, shipping operators, maritime unions

for.name: Rep. Justin Amash
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Jones Act; it was his measure alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over maritime law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 17, 2020 and sent it to a subcommittee, but took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough support for a partisan fight: it had a single Independent sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken.

industries.note: U.S. shipyards sell their large commercial vessels almost entirely into the Jones Act-protected market, where buyers must use American-built ships at far higher prices than foreign yards charge. Repeal would open that closed market; defeat keeps the shipyards' guaranteed customer base intact, with the cost spread across shipping rates paid by consumers.

industries.industry: U.S.-flag shipping operators and merchant mariners
industries.note: Jones Act carriers hold domestic cargo routes to themselves and charge higher rates than foreign competition would, and their American crews earn wages the bill's repeal would expose to competition. The military also draws on this fleet for sealift, which is the strongest public-interest argument for keeping it.

industries.industry: Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska consumers and businesses
industries.note: These markets are served almost entirely by ocean shipping and bear the steepest Jones Act cost premium. Repeal would have let cheaper foreign vessels compete for their cargo, lowering freight costs that show up in retail prices.
